newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU finance ministers in crisis talks on lira.
newsitem.headline: EU finance ministers in crisis talks on lira.

text.p: Finance ministers and central bank governors from the European Union met in emergency session Sunday to decide how to bring the Italian lira into the EU's exchange rate mechanism after a four-year absence.

Europe's top financial policy-makers had to be called in after a Saturday meeting of the EU's monetary committee of central bank and finance ministry officials failed to agree on a central rate for the lira's return.

Italy, which on Saturday was hoping for a rate of 1,010 lira to the German mark, lowered its sights to 1,000 Sunday in an attempt to win agreement, but it still had not won over its EU partners, a diplomat said.
"The Italians are proposing to come down to 1,000 (lira to the German mark)," a diplomat said, referring to the central rate at which the lira would enter the EU's currency grid.
A Spanish official said Italy's partners were seeking a rate of between 950 to 980 lira to the mark.
"Italy is willing to go to 1,000. Other countries are seeking 950 to 980," the diplomat said, adding that no deal was in sight.
Germany in particular was objecting, arguing that the Italian government was trying to bring the lira back into the ERM at a weak rate, the diplomat said.
"The Germans are not happy," he said.

Luxembourg Finance Minister Jean-Claude Juncker, who is also the country's prime minister, said he was not surprised that the lower-level body had failed to agree on Saturday because the issue had far-reaching political consequences.

"This is a political debate," he told reporters as he entered the Sunday meeting. "I don't think the monetary committee was the appropriate body for formulating an answer to a problem which is eminently political.
"The problem is whether or not we want to put Italy into a position where it fulfils one of the Maastricht criteria," for joining a unified European currency, he said.

Rejoining the exchange rate mechanism -- from which the lira was unceremoniously dumped amid a currency crisis in 1992 -- is seen as crucial for Italy's hopes for being in the first wave of EU countries to adopt the single currency in 1999.
A stable two-year stint within the ERM -- designed to provide exchange rate stability -- is one of the qualifying criteria for the new currency, the Euro.
Rome, officials said, was asking for lira to come in at too weak a level, worrying other European countries that this would give Italy preferential trade terms.
Italy's failure to win a seat within the exchange rate mechanism could put pressure on the lira and send a strong negative signal over the prospect of a joint European currency.
But Italy was not in a strong position at the meeting because of what might happen to the lira if it was not let back in at all.
France has been the most vehement in wanting a stronger rate for the lira, having seen some of its trade battered by a neighbour with a weaker currency.
Italy, like other EU countries that want to join the monetary union from the start, has rushed to meet targets on interest and exchange rates, inflation, the budget deficit and public debt.
Seeking to trim their deficits next year to no more than 3 percent of gross domestic product, however, some states have unveiled controversial one-time budgetary measures.
Italy has proposed a so-called "Euro-tax," a one-time revenue raiser to help it meet the targets.
If Italy is brought into the exchange rate mechanism, only three of the EU's 15 countries will be outside the grid.
Britain and Sweden argue that it is not necessary to be in the grid to qualify for the Euro, it is enough to have a stable rate with the other countries.
Both countries are sceptical about the Euro project.
Greece's economy is far weaker than the others and membership of the single currency is far off.
